wellness-pillars.label: Wellness Pillars
wellness-pillars.title: Pillars of Brain Health
wellness-pillars.description: Four scientifically proven habits that support neural connectivity and delay cognitive ageing.

items.title: Nutrition
items.text: A diet rich in antioxidants, omega-3 fatty acids and green vegetables protects brain cells and supports micro-vascular circulation.

items.title: Physical Activity
items.text: Regular aerobic exercise increases blood flow to the brain, encourages neuroplasticity and releases BDNF, which supports memory cells.

items.title: Restful Sleep
items.text: Deep sleep activates the brain's glymphatic system, clearing metabolic waste and proteins such as amyloid-beta that drive cognitive decline.

items.title: Mental Exercise
items.text: Learning new skills, reading, solving puzzles and staying socially active builds cognitive reserve that resists age-related memory loss.

fast-signs.label: FAST Warning Signs
fast-signs.title: Act F.A.S.T. - Learn the Signs
fast-signs.description: If you observe any of these symptoms in yourself or someone else, call the emergency stroke helpline immediately.

items.title: Face Drooping
items.text: Does one side of the face droop or is it numb? Ask the person to smile. Is the smile uneven?

items.title: Arm Weakness
items.text: Is one arm weak or numb? Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift downward?

items.title: Speech Difficulty
items.text: Is speech slurred? Is the person unable to speak or hard to understand? Ask them to repeat a simple sentence.

items.title: Time to Call Help
items.text: If the person shows any of these signs, even if the symptoms go away, check the time and call us immediately.

golden-hour.label: Golden Hour Protocol
golden-hour.title: Golden Hour Window
golden-hour.description: When a stroke strikes, millions of brain cells die every minute. Reversing this damage is highly dependent on how quickly blood flow is restored.

items.text: Within 4.5 Hours: Clot-dissolving IV thrombolysis injection can be administered to open blocked arteries.
Within 24 Hours: Advanced mechanical thrombectomy (catheter-guided clot removal) can save patients with large blood vessel blockages.

while-waiting.label: While Waiting for the Ambulance
while-waiting.title: What to Do While Waiting for the Ambulance

items.text: Keep the patient calm and lay them down on their side (recovery position) if they are unconscious or vomiting.
DO NOT give any food, water, or aspirin. Swallowing reflexes are often impaired during a stroke, posing a severe choking hazard.
Note down the exact time when you first observed symptoms. This is crucial for selecting the right treatment protocol.

types.label: Types of Seizures
types.title: Types of Seizures
types.description: Understanding the different types of seizures is crucial for proper diagnosis and treatment. Seizures are categorized based on where they begin in the brain.

items.title: Focal Onset Seizures
items.text: Begin in one area of the brain. May cause changes in sensation, emotions, or movements while the person remains conscious (focal aware) or may cause loss of awareness (focal impaired awareness).

items.title: Generalized Onset Seizures
items.text: Affect both sides of the brain simultaneously from the start. These include absence seizures (brief loss of awareness), tonic seizures (muscle stiffening), and clonic seizures (rhythmic jerking).

items.title: Unknown Onset Seizures
items.text: When the beginning of a seizure cannot be determined as focal or generalized. Further testing and monitoring may be needed to classify the seizure type accurately.

types.label: Common Headache Types
types.title: Common Headache Types
types.description: Headaches are classified as primary (not caused by another condition) or secondary (caused by an underlying health problem).

items.title: Tension Headache
items.text: The most common type, causing a constant dull ache or feeling of tight band pressure around the forehead, back of the head, and neck. Usually related to stress or muscle tension.

items.title: Cluster Headache
items.text: Severe, piercing pain that occurs in cycles or clusters, usually concentrated around one eye. Often accompanied by watering of the eye, nasal congestion, and restlessness.

items.title: Secondary Headache
items.text: Headaches resulting from other medical conditions, such as sinus infections, dental problems, high blood pressure, head injuries, or blood vessel issues in the brain.

types.label: Types of Migraines
types.title: Types of Migraines
types.description: Migraines are classified depending on the presence of sensory warning signs called auras.

items.title: Migraine with Aura
items.text: Preceded by visual flashes, blind spots, tingling in hands/face, or temporary speech issues about 10-60 minutes before the headache begins.

items.title: Migraine without Aura
items.text: The most common type. Severe, throbbing, one-sided pain occurs without prior warning signs, lasting 4-72 hours if left untreated.

items.title: Chronic Migraine
items.text: Diagnosed when headaches occur on 15 or more days a month for at least 3 months, with at least 8 of those days presenting as typical migraines.

types.label: Common Movement Disorders
types.title: Common Movement Disorders
types.description: Movement disorders present as involuntary muscle twitching, steady shaking, or a lack of coordination.

items.title: Essential Tremor
items.text: A common nerve disorder causing involuntary shaking, typically in the hands during active tasks like writing, drinking, or holding objects.

items.title: Dystonia
items.text: Causes involuntary muscle contractions, leading to repetitive twisting movements or abnormal postures (such as writer's cramp or cervical neck twisting).

items.title: Ataxia
items.text: A degenerative condition affecting the cerebellum, resulting in a severe lack of voluntary muscle coordination, balance problems, and unsteady walking.

types.label: Types of Multiple Sclerosis
types.title: Types of Multiple Sclerosis
types.description: Multiple Sclerosis manifests differently in each patient, following distinct progression patterns.

items.title: Relapsing-Remitting MS (RRMS)
items.text: The most common form (85% of cases). Defined by clear relapses (attacks) followed by periods of remission where symptoms resolve completely or partially.

items.title: Primary Progressive MS (PPMS)
items.text: Steady worsening of symptoms from the onset without distinct relapses or remissions. Typically diagnosed in patients after age 40.

items.title: Secondary Progressive (SPMS)
items.text: Follows an initial relapsing-remitting course. Over time, the disease transitions into a progressive phase with steady worsening of symptoms between attacks.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Multiple Sclerosis
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Multiple Sclerosis
diagnosis.description: Since there is no single test for MS, diagnosis requires proving "dissemination in time and space"—lesions in different brain areas occurring at different times.

items.title: Clinical Evaluation
items.text: A detailed history of neurological symptoms, relapses, and physical exams tracking sensory and motor nerve deficits.

items.title: Brain & Spine MRI
items.text: High-resolution scans using contrast dye to detect active and scarred lesions (plaques) within myelin structures.

items.title: Lumbar Puncture
items.text: Analyzing spinal fluid to look for oligoclonal bands or specific immunoglobulins indicative of an active CNS immune response.

items.title: Evoked Potentials
items.text: Testing the speed of electrical signals traveling through visual or sensory nerve pathways to detect myelin slowing.

items.title: Autoimmune Origin
items.text: Immune system attacks myelin

items.title: DMT Availability
items.text: Modern drugs slow progression

items.title: Variable Course
items.text: Relapsing and progressive types

be-fast.label: BE-FAST Warning Signs
be-fast.title: BE FAST: Stroke Recognition
be-fast.description: Use the BE FAST method to immediately identify stroke symptoms in others and coordinate care.

items.title: Balance & Eyes
items.text: Sudden loss of balance, trouble walking, or coordination difficulty, paired with abrupt vision changes like blurred or double vision.

items.title: Face & Arms
items.text: One side of the face droops or is numb when attempting to smile. When raising both arms, one arm drifts downward or feels weak.

items.title: Speech & Time
items.text: Speech is slurred, garbled, or difficult to understand, or the person cannot speak. Time is critical  call the emergency helpline immediately.

emergency-protocol.label: Emergency Protocol
emergency-protocol.title: Our Emergency Response Protocol
emergency-protocol.description: Our emergency neurology protocol coordinates fast-tracked diagnostics and treatments to save brain tissue.

items.title: Rapid Brain Imaging
items.text: Upon arrival at emergency, a non-contrast brain CT scan is performed within 25 minutes to verify the type of stroke.

items.title: IV Thrombolysis
items.text: Clot-dissolving medication (tPA) is administered intravenously to break down blockages and restore blood circulation.

items.title: Mechanical Retrieval
items.text: Catheter-based thrombectomy is performed in our Cath Lab to physically extract the blockage from the cerebral artery.

items.title: ICU Care & Tracking
items.text: Transfer to the specialized Neuro-ICU for continuous intracranial pressure, blood pressure, and EEG monitoring.

symptom-cards.label: Symptoms Directory
symptom-cards.title: Identify Your Symptoms
symptom-cards.description: Click on the symptom areas below to learn about potential underlying conditions and when to see a specialist.

items.title: Chronic / Severe Headaches
items.text: Recurrent throbbing, sharp headaches, or headaches accompanied by nausea, sensitivity to light/sound, or visual disturbances.
items.subtitle: Potential Causes: Migraine, Tension Headache, Cluster Headache.

items.title: Dizziness & Loss of Balance
items.text: Feeling lightheaded, unsteady, or experiencing a spinning sensation (vertigo) which affects coordination or walking.
items.subtitle: Potential Causes: Vestibular Vertigo, Balance disorders, Inner-ear infection.

items.title: Numbness & Tingling
items.text: A "pins and needles" sensation, loss of feeling, or burning pain in the feet, legs, hands, or arms.
items.subtitle: Potential Causes: Peripheral Neuropathy, Radiculopathy, Nerve entrapment.

items.title: Tremors & Stiffness
items.text: Involuntary shaking of the hands or limbs, muscle stiffness, slowed movements, or difficulty with walking coordination.
items.subtitle: Potential Causes: Parkinson's Disease, Essential Tremor, Movement disorders.

items.title: Memory Loss & Confusion
items.text: Persistent forgetfulness, difficulty finding words, disorientation in familiar places, or sudden changes in cognitive behavior.
items.subtitle: Potential Causes: Dementia, Early-onset Alzheimer's, Vitamin deficiencies, Neurodegeneration.

items.title: Muscle Weakness
items.text: Loss of muscle power, difficulty raising arms or legs, foot drop, or general weakness that worsens with activity.
items.subtitle: Potential Causes: Multiple Sclerosis, Myopathies, Motor neuron diseases.

red-flags.label: Red Flag Warnings
red-flags.title: When is it a Neurological Emergency?
red-flags.description: Some symptoms indicate acute damage or severe threat to the nervous system. If you notice any of these signs, seek emergency care immediately.

items.text: Sudden weakness or numbness in the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side of the body.
Sudden speech difficulty, slurring, confusion, or difficulty understanding others.
Worst headache of your life (sudden onset "thunderclap" headache).
Loss of vision or double vision occurring suddenly.

red-flags.panel_text: Under the clinical directorship of Dr. Praveen Gupta, Marengo Asia Hospital operates a dedicated 24/7 emergency stroke and seizure response protocol.

types.label: Neuropathy Categories
types.title: Neuropathy Categories
types.description: Nerve damage is classified by its underlying trigger, guiding our targeted treatment approach.

items.title: Diabetic Neuropathy
items.text: The most common form. High blood sugars over time damage small blood vessels that feed peripheral nerves, resulting in chronic numbness or burning in the feet.

items.title: Inflammatory Neuropathies
items.text: Autoimmune attacks on peripheral myelin. Includes acute Guillain-BarrÃ© Syndrome (GBS) and chronic CIDP, presenting with rapidly progressive muscle weakness.

items.title: Nutritional & Toxic Neuropathy
items.text: Nerve damage due to vitamin deficiencies (such as B12, B1, or B6), chronic alcohol consumption, heavy metals, or chemotherapy drugs.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Neuropathy
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Neuropathy
diagnosis.description: Diagnosing peripheral neuropathy involves checking electrical conduction speed inside nerves, combined with lab screens to pinpoint root causes.

items.title: EMG & NCV Studies
items.text: Nerve Conduction Velocity (NCV) tests and Electromyography (EMG) measure electrical activity in muscles to locate nerve compression or damage.

items.title: Metabolic Lab Tests
items.text: Comprehensive blood screens checking HbA1c (diabetes), vitamin B12 levels, thyroid markers, renal functions, and autoantibodies.

items.title: Quantitative Sensory
items.text: Sensory testing checking temperature shifts, touch thresholds, and vibration limits to identify large vs. small nerve fiber damage.

items.title: Skin Biopsy
items.text: A minimally invasive, 3mm punch skin biopsy to check intraepidermal nerve fiber density, confirming small fiber neuropathy.

items.title: Peripheral Nerves
items.text: Connects spinal cord to limbs

items.title: Diabetic Connection
items.text: Diabetes is the leading cause

items.title: Nerve Regeneration
items.text: Nerves can heal with care

symptoms.title: Neuropathy Symptoms
symptoms.description: Neuropathy symptoms vary depending on whether sensory, motor, or autonomic nerves are damaged.
symptoms.note_text: Autonomic nerve damage can disrupt internal systems, causing heat intolerance, abnormal sweating, and fluctuations in blood pressure or heart rate.

vascular-conditions.label: Vascular Conditions Managed
vascular-conditions.title: Vascular Conditions Managed
vascular-conditions.description: Each of these conditions carries a risk of sudden, catastrophic bleeding — which is why they are treated as time-critical.

items.title: Cerebral Aneurysms
items.text: Preventing subarachnoid haemorrhage — bleeding around the brain — by securing the weak point through clipping or coiling.

items.title: Arteriovenous Malformations
items.text: Resecting or embolising complex tangles of arteries and veins before they rupture and bleed into brain tissue.

items.title: Carotid Stenosis
items.text: Carotid endarterectomy or stenting to reopen the narrowed neck arteries that supply the brain, preventing acute stroke.

items.title: Treatment Planning
items.text: The team decides between open microsurgery and an endovascular approach based on the location, size and shape of the lesion.

items.title: Intervention
items.text: Surgical clipping under the microscope, or micro-catheters fed from the groin for coiling, stent-assisted reconstruction or flow diversion.

types.label: Parkinsonian Disorders
types.title: Parkinsonian Disorders
types.description: Symptoms of slowness and tremors can be caused by idiopathic Parkinson's disease or other look-alike syndromes.

items.title: Idiopathic Parkinson's
items.text: The classic form of the disease. Responsive to levodopa therapy. Primary symptoms include resting tremors, muscle stiffness, and slowness.

items.title: Parkinson-Plus
items.text: Syndromes like Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) or Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) that present with tremors but have additional symptoms and progress differently.

items.title: Drug-Induced
items.text: Reversible parkinsonism symptoms caused by certain medications (such as antipsychotics) that block dopamine receptors in the brain.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Parkinson's
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Parkinson's
diagnosis.description: Diagnosing Parkinson's relies primarily on expert clinical observation of motor patterns, reflexes, and response to specific dopaminergic drugs.

items.title: Clinical Evaluation
items.text: Expert examination of resting tremors, motor rigidity, postural balance, and gait patterns.

items.title: Drug Challenge
items.text: Assessing physical response to Levodopa medication. A significant improvement in motor speed supports a Parkinson's diagnosis.

items.title: DaTscan Imaging
items.text: Dopamine Transporter SPECT scan tracing dopamine pathways in the brain to confirm neurodegenerative drop-offs.

items.title: Brain MRI
items.text: High-resolution imaging scans to rule out atypical parkinsonism, strokes, fluid blockages, or brain stem abnormalities.

items.title: Neurodegenerative
items.text: Dopamine neuron loss in brain

items.title: Gradual Progression
items.text: Develops slowly over years

items.title: DBS Option
items.text: Neurosurgery blocks motor tremors

items.title: Physical Therapy
items.text: Helps maintain motor controls

symptoms.label: Symptoms & Warning Signs
symptoms.title: Symptoms & Warning Signs
symptoms.description: Parkinson's symptoms are divided into motor symptoms (affecting physical movement) and non-motor symptoms (affecting sensory, mood, or sleep functions).
symptoms.note_text: Intervening early with dopamine agonists or levodopa can slow motor decline and preserve independent functioning for years.

items.title: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS)

types.label: Types of Stroke
types.title: Types of Stroke
types.description: Strokes are divided into categories based on whether they involve blood vessel blockage or rupture.

items.title: Ischemic Stroke
items.text: The most common type (accounts for 87% of strokes). Caused by a blood clot blocking an artery that supplies blood to the brain, cutting off oxygen.

items.title: Hemorrhagic Stroke
items.text: Occurs when a weakened blood vessel ruptures and leaks blood into the surrounding brain tissue, causing severe local pressure and damage.

items.title: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
items.text: Known as a "mini-stroke." Blood flow is blocked temporarily (often resolving within minutes). Although symptoms fade quickly, a TIA is a warning sign of an impending major stroke.

diagnosis.label: How We Diagnose Stroke
diagnosis.title: How We Diagnose Stroke
diagnosis.description: Emergency diagnostics are completed within minutes of arrival to determine if a stroke is ischemic or hemorrhagic, guiding immediate intervention.

items.title: Rapid Neuro Exam
items.text: Immediate clinical checking of sensory inputs, pupillary reflexes, speech clarity, and motor strengths to assess severity.

items.title: Emergency Brain CT
items.text: Fast imaging to rule out brain bleeding (hemorrhage) before prescribing blood thinners or clot-busting medications.

items.title: Brain MRI & MRA
items.text: Detailed imaging scan to trace exact brain tissue damage locations and map arterial blood flow pathways.

items.title: Vascular Ultrasound
items.text: Carotid duplex ultrasound checks for narrow neck arteries or plaques that could spark subsequent strokes.

items.title: Brain Attack
items.text: Requires emergency response

items.title: Time Sensitive
items.text: "Time is Brain" - act FAST

items.title: Preventable

types.label: Common Vertigo Types
types.title: Common Vertigo Types
types.description: Vertigo is categorized based on whether the origin is inside the inner ear balance canals or the brain.

items.title: BPPV
items.text: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo. Triggered by specific head movements, caused by tiny calcium carbonate crystals displacing into the inner ear fluid canals.

items.title: Peripheral Vertigo
items.text: Originates in the inner ear balance nerves. Common causes include vestibular neuritis (viral infection of the nerve) and Meniere's disease (fluid build-up in the ear).

items.title: Central Vertigo
items.text: Originates in the brainstem or cerebellum. Triggered by conditions like vestibular migraines, strokes, tumors, or multiple sclerosis.

diagnosis.label: Diagnosing Vertigo
diagnosis.title: Diagnosing Vertigo
diagnosis.description: Diagnosing vertigo involves checking both your balance systems and inner ear fluid pathways to identify positional triggers.

items.title: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver
items.text: A clinical movement test to trigger positional nystagmus (involuntary eye movement) and verify BPPV in the canals.

items.title: Vestibular Testing
items.text: Video-nystagmography (VNG) tests and caloric stimulation check inner ear balance responses.

items.title: Brain MRI
items.text: High-resolution imaging to rule out brainstem strokes, multiple sclerosis plaques, acoustic neuromas, or tumors.

items.title: Hearing Evaluation
items.text: Audiometry screening to rule out Meniere's disease or acoustic nerve issues that affect hearing pathways.

items.title: Balance System
items.text: Linked to inner ear & brain

items.title: Often Drug-Free
items.text: Relieved by body maneuvers

items.title: Common Causes
items.text: BPPV is the main culprit

items.title: Therapeutic Rehab
items.text: Vestibular retraining works

warning.title: When to Seek Emergency Care
warning.description: Seek immediate medical attention if vertigo is accompanied by:

items.text: Double vision or blurred vision
Slurred speech or difficulty talking
Weakness or numbness in arms or legs
Difficulty walking or loss of coordination

symptoms.title: Vertigo Symptoms
symptoms.description: Vertigo presents with a spinning sensation that can trigger physical and sensory reflexes in the body.
symptoms.note_text: Symptoms are typically exacerbated by head movements, rolling over in bed, tilting the head upward, or sudden posture shifts.

treatments.label: Treatment Options
treatments.title: Comprehensive Vertigo Treatment Options
treatments.description: Many types of vertigo can be resolved without pills. We offer targeted maneuvers and custom physical rehabilitation therapies.

items.title: Canalith Repositioning (Epley Maneuver)
items.subtitle: Drug-free physical crystal resetting
items.text: For BPPV sufferers, a series of structured head movements guided by the doctor rolls floating ear crystals back into place, providing relief.

items.title: Vestibular Rehabilitation Therapy (VRT)
items.subtitle: Retraining balance & stabilizing gaze
items.text: Custom exercises designed to help your brain compensate for inner ear abnormalities, improving stability and reducing fall risk.

items.title: Pharmacological Therapies
items.subtitle: Vestibular suppressants & anti-emetics
items.text: Medications can help control severe acute symptoms of dizziness and nausea during flare-ups or viral infections of the vestibular nerve.

items.title: Diet & Safety Guidance
items.subtitle: Low-sodium dietary support & safety checks
items.text: For Meniere's disease, dietary fluid control (limiting salt and caffeine) helps manage pressure build-up in the inner ear canals.
